Continued intensive study of German at the intermediate level: reading, writing, speaking, listening, and cultural contexts. Lessons are taught in an authentic cultural context.

subject: GER
title: First-Year Seminar in German
description: This seminar will introduce students to the study of German, Austrian, Swiss, Yiddish and/or Dutch literature, film and culture in their first year at Penn State. Students will read significant texts (in English), view videos (with subtitles), listen to music and explore Germanic-speaking cultures in general. These experiences will help prepare students for additional courses in literature and in German as well as provide a point of comparison with U.S. culture. Specific topics or themes for the course may vary from semester to semester. In addition to the academic topic explored in this course, students can expect to gain a general introduction to the University as an academic community and have the opportunity to explore their responsibilities as members of that community. Students will develop an understanding of the learning tools and resources available to them including the opportunity to develop relationships with faculty and other students who share their academic interests.

subject: GER
title: Foreign Study--German
description: Courses offered in foreign countries by individual or group instruction.

subject: GER
title: German Culture and Civilization
description: German 100 provides a cultural history of Germany, Switzerland, and Austria from the Roman Empire to the Nazi defeat. Readings and discussions will be in English. The class examines the role of German tribes in the collapse of Rome, the emergence of a powerful medieval Empire, the architecture and devotions of Romanesque and Gothic cathedrals, the rise of manufacturing cities, the art of the Northern Renaissance, Martin Luther and the Protestant Reformation, Catholic Responses, The Thirty Years War, the Absolute King and the ban on sectarian warfare, the Rise of Prussia as a military monarchy, the Enlightenment, Napoleon and the end of the Holy Roman Empire, German Romanticism and Nationalism, Industrialization, the 1848 Revolution, Unification, Ethnic nationalism in the Austro-Hungarian Empire, World War One, Empires collapse, the Weimar Republic, Inflation, the Versailles Treaty, Modern art, Nazi seizure dictatorship, racial policy and the Holocaust, World War Two, Nazi defeat. Readings will include historical documents and a history textbook. Short discussions of art, architecture, music, literature, and philosophy are included. The class is organized around lectures, with visual aids and class screenings of films. The course is designed to be suitable for all students generally interested in German, or interested in various fields of humanistic study, whether or not they have previously studied the culture of Germany. This course is designed to fulfill General Education GH "General Humanities," IL "International Cultures," and also BA requirements.
attributes: GLO: Soc Resp and Ethic Reason

subject: GER
title: Science, Humanity and Catastrophe: Scientific Discovery in Germany
description: The 20th century was a time of great scientific advancement - advancements that were used both for good and for evil (and for other purposes that lie somewhere in between). Germany and German-speaking scientists played central roles in many of these discoveries. In this course we will take an interdisciplinary approach to discussing key scientific advancements, including the discovery of nuclear fission and the development of the nuclear bomb, the discovery of polymers and the invention of pain medicines such as morphine and oxycodone, learning about the science behind these discoveries alongside the social and historical contexts in which they occurred, and the impact these discoveries had on society. While a majority of the scientific discoveries that we will focus on took place in the first half of the 20th century, we will also discuss the ways in which the long-term consequences of these discoveries are still relevant today, especially as they relate to current issues on sustainability (e.g., the use of plastics) and the ethical considerations that arise more generally when thinking about the relationship between science, technology, engineering and society.
attributes: GLO: Soc Resp and Ethic Reason

subject: GER
title: Genocide in Global perspectives: Twentieth Century and beyond
description: The history and memory of the Holocaust, the Armenian, Cambodian and other forms of genocide are often taught separately in different disciplines. This course will examine them together through the various ways different societies dealt with, experienced and understood these. Using the extensive literature on the history of genocide this course further suggests ways in which these tragic events affected and were entangled by each other's. Specific content will vary according to individual instructor, but topics may include victim cultures, ethnic cleansing, trauma, human rights, dark tourism, memorials, architecture as well as the general impact of these tragedies on global politics, or the way the memories of the tragedies were entangled with the civil rights and other struggles in American and global history.
attributes: GLO: Soc Resp and Ethic Reason

subject: GER
title: The Holocaust in Film and Literature
description: This class studies how art, literature, film, and other media can help us to gain a perspective on one of the most horrific events in human history, the Holocaust: the genocidal murder of more than six million men, women, and children (mostly Jewish) under the Nazi regime during World War II. We will also examine the theoretical questions involved in any attempt to capture what appears to be beyond our comprehension, in terms of moral outrage and the sheer scale, inhumanity, and bureaucratic efficiency. To this end we will study literary works, such as Primo Levi's Survival in Auschwitz, films such as Steven Spielberg's Schindler's List, Roman Polanski's The Pianist, and Roberto Benigni's Life is Beautiful, as well as photographs, poems, artworks, installations, museum architecture, the design of monuments and other artifacts. We will also examine questions of memorialization (Holocaust museums and memorials), national guilt, survivor's guilt, stigmatization, and the ethics of historical representation.
attributes: GLO: Soc Resp and Ethic Reason

subject: GER
title: Gender and Sexuality in Weimar Berlin, 1918 - 1933
description: This course engages with why Weimar Berlin was a unique and important moment in the Western history of gender and sexuality. This course introduces students to topics in gender and sexuality in media, literature, film and their cultural context in Weimar Berlin. Students will explore how gender was policed in Weimar Berlin and the ways in which medical, political, and artistic institutions became involved with people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities. Students will discuss the ways in which certain behaviors or lifestyles were allowed to exist in public spaces for the first time, on the one hand, but also how this the Nazis used this knowledge in the following decades. Students will analyze how Berlin between 1918-1933 served as a significant hub for queer and gay subcultures and who the prominent figures in this cultural era were.

subject: GER
title: The Culture of Stalinism and Nazism
description: This course, which is cross-listed between Russian and German, aims to acquaint students with an important and troubling chapter of 20th-century culture. The regimes of Stalin and Hitler have had a decisive impact not only on life in Russia and Germany, but in much of Europe and the world at large. Espousing a comparative perspective, the course explores the culture produced by Stalinist Russia and Nazi Germany, considering both the culture of daily life and selected works of "high culture," including literature, the visual arts, architecture, music, and film. A knowledge of Russian or German is not required, as class lectures and discussions as well as all reading assignments are in English.
attributes: GLO: Soc Resp and Ethic Reason

subject: GER
title: The Amish
description: This course surveys the history, culture, religion, and society of the Amish and related Anabaptist sectarian groups in North America. The course focuses on basic human issues, such as family, community, and economy, and the values that inform the Amish approach to these issues. Students will gain an understanding of their beliefs and values, i.e., why they often travel by horse and buggy and generally do not have electricity in their homes. This course also cultivates students' knowledge about the social and religious identity of the Amish. This course is suitable for students interested in several diverse topics ranging from agriculture, anthropology, history, and religious studies.
attributes: GLO: Soc Resp and Ethic Reason

subject: GER
title: Marx, Nietzsche, Freud
description: In this course you will learn about three controversial thinkers of modern life. We will turn to German philosophy and psychology to examine basic questions that trouble us today. Karl Marx will help us understand: How does capitalism actually work? How are profits produced? What forms of exploitation are built into industrial labor? How did globalization begin? Sigmund Freud's invention of psychoanalysis will show us: How sexual drives shape our personalities? What is the unconscious and how does it appear in our daily lives? What do dreams tell us about ourselves? The radical ideas of Friedrich Nietzsche will challenge: What is truth? How does it serve power? What are the foundations of Christian morality? Does God exist? In this course you will learn how each thinker altered the course of modern history through their distinctive methods and questions. You will learn why they were each so revolutionary and how important they are for our own era. All texts and discussion are in English.

subject: GER
title: Germanic Heroic and Medieval Literature in English Translation
description: In this course, students will become able to describe the complex cultural history of the German-speaking Middle Ages and its modern reception through analysis of literary and cultural production. The period between the Germanic migrations of the fourth century C.E. (Common Era) and the waning of the high Middle Ages around 1250 C.E. was shaped by a complex convergence of sociocultural, theological, and political forces. A shift from the agrarian society of early Germanic peoples with a minimal government structure, to the stratified socio-political system of the High Middle Ages is reflected in written documents and literary production of the time. Evolving and emerging value systems often clashed. For instance, knights were expected to be the warriors depicted in heroic epic and yet also to behave like the civilized courtiers of Arthurian Romance. Modern retellings of Arthurian and heroic stories are popular in modern film and literature. Newer scholarly approaches such as culture theory, gender studies, critical race theory, and post-colonial studies have expanded the available tools for analysis of Germanic medieval literature and culture. Students will examine historical documents, literary works, visual art, music, as well as secondary articles on history, culture, and literature and will discuss the complexity and diversity of this time period in German-speaking regions. Using modern tools of analysis, students will compare the medieval material with its reception in modern cultural production and will evaluate the relevance of medieval culture to modern society.

subject: GER
title: German Film
description: A survey of German film from its beginnings to the present, with emphasis on historical, political, and cultural contexts. The course also equips students with the basic tools of film criticism and engages salient questions related to visual cultures, past and present, to develop skills for critical spectatorship in a world dominated by images.

subject: GER
title: Twentieth-Century German Literature in English Translation
description: This course introduces students to literature written in German in the twentieth century, including by authors living in German-speaking countries such as Austria, Germany, and Switzerland, but also by writers in exile or from outside of these regions. Though organizing genres and/or topics may vary, students will learn to read texts in relation to (and as a way better to understand) the dramatically shifting social and political contexts of their production. All texts and discussions are in English.

subject: GER
title: Special Topics

subject: GER
title: Foreign Study--German
description: Intermediate training in German language skills.

subject: GER
title: Contemporary German Culture
description: How do we make sense of Germany, the country's history, culture, politics, and economics during the twentieth century? In modern German history, periods of impressive social, political, economic, cultural, and intellectual achievements alternated with times of violence, destruction, two world wars, genocide, and authoritarian structures in politics and society. This course helps students to understand Germany during the 20th century. The main focal points of this course include World War I, the 1918 revolution followed by the short history of the Weimar Republic, the rise of the Nazis and the Third Reich, World War II and the Holocaust, post-war reconstruction, the foundation of two German states in 1949, their development until (re-) unification in 1990, the development of Germany from unification to today, Germany's current dominant economic position within the EU, and the recent rise of radical right-wing politics in Germany for the first time since 1945. These focal areas will be approached from various perspectives: From historical (and historiographical) vantage points, from sociological and economic perspectives, and through the lenses of cultural productions such as novels, movies, and other works of art.

subject: GER
title: Conversation and Composition
description: Continuation of GER 3. Developing reading, writing, listening and speaking skills in German through content-based tasks that focus on different aspects of German culture. Class and homework activities also provide additional practice and review of German grammar.

subject: GER
title: The Vikings
description: The Vikings will study the rise and proliferation of Viking culture and society during the Viking Age (c. 793 - c. 1066 CE). This course will examine Norse/Scandinavian culture including their social structure, political and economic systems, technology (especially shipbuilding and navigation), religion, literature, language and of course the raiding, trading and exploration traditionally associated with Vikings. As the course synthesizes and analyzes historical evidence, several themes will be of importance including: social and economic structures, religious belief systems, the place of women and marginalized groups in society, and cultural developments such as art and literature. The overall goal of this course is to use factual and thematic knowledge of this time period and these cultures to analyze and appreciate both change and continuity in the development of Viking history.
attributes: GLO: Soc Resp and Ethic Reason

subject: GER
title: Intermediate Speaking and Listening
description: Intensive practice to improve listening comprehension and spoken German through readings, discussions and video.

subject: GER
title: Intermediate Composition and Grammar
description: Continuation of oral and written practice in German with extensive work in composition. Fundamental to the course is a thorough review of basic and advanced grammatical situations, with the goal of improving students' grammatical and stylistic precision in written German discourse across a variety of genres.

subject: GER
title: German Business Communication
description: This course provides an introduction to German, Austrian and Swiss business and economics. Students will read and respond to a variety of texts about topics, such as German economic practices and the German business world, Germany and the European Union, the German job market, as well as texts that introduce and describe more general economic principles and current events. Emphasis is also placed on expanding students' vocabulary and further developing their writing skills in German, especially with regards to economic and business terminology, and writing genres common in business contexts. This course is conducted primarily in German

subject: GER
title: Introduction to the Study of German Literature
description: History, methods, and the terminology of literary interpretation and analysis in German.

subject: GER
title: Intermediate German Culture
description: An overview of German culture from the Middle Ages to the present. Conducted in German. GER 344 Intermediate German Culture (3) (IL) This course will be a comprehensive overview of major events and figures in German history that have influenced the development of German culture. This will be a foundational course that will enable students to better situate advanced courses in German literature and culture in the broader context of a cultural tradition that stretches from the Germanic migrations to the present. The course will be taught in German at the intermediate level and will be required of all German majors and minors. It will be a prerequisite for culture courses taught in German at the 400-level. Students will be evaluated on the basis of written tests, an oral presentation and essay on a major cultural figure or event, homework, and class participation. The course will be offered every semester. The enrollment for each section will be capped at approximately 22.

subject: GER
title: Foreign Study--German
description: Advanced studies in German language and/or literature.

subject: GER
title: Advanced Composition
description: Advanced study of the German language with emphasis on complex grammatical structures, consolidation of vocabulary, cultural knowledge, and intensive practice of written communication skills.

subject: GER
title: Introduction to German Literature in Cultural Context
description: In this course we will read and analyze an array of literary texts and visual media (e.g., art, films or other audio-visual media) to answer questions such as: 1) What are the key historical epochs, literary periods, and political organizations that define the history of the German-speaking world and who are some of its key figures and authors? 2) How do political events and trends create new genres? And how are politics, literary movements, and genres connected? 3) Through which historical processes did the modern German, Austrian and Swiss nations arise? In addition to learning how to interpret literary text and visual media in their cultural context, students will have the opportunity for intensive practice in spoken and written German. This course is taught primarily in German.

subject: GER
title: Advanced German Business Communications
description: This course provides more advanced engagement with topics related to German, Austrian and Swiss business. Topics may include German business organization, forms of business communication, German finance and the DAX and current events, especially as they relate to Germany in a global world. Emphasis is also placed on expanding students' vocabulary and writing skills in German, especially as they relate to business terminology and international business contexts. This course is conducted primarily in German.

subject: GER
title: The Teaching of German
description: This course is designed to foster an informed professional outlook on the teaching and learning of foreign languages in general and German in particular. Students will learn about common concepts and terminology within the field of second language acquisition, and how this area of research informs foreign language pedagogy and vice versa. Both during and outside of class, students will also learn about the practical side of foreign language teaching, including the development of lesson plans, writing and grading quizzes and exams, and evaluating oneself as a teacher. This course is conducted primarily in German

subject: GER
title: Introduction to German linguistics
description: This course provides an overview of the structure of the German language from its sound system (phonetics and phonology) to word formation (morphology) and word order (syntax), to language variation (sociolinguistics) and language change (historical linguistics). The overview will include comparisons with other Germanic languages such as English. This course is taught in German.

subject: GER
title: Genre
description: Special studies in a particular literary genre in German literature, such as lyrical poetry, drama, or narrative prose.

subject: GER
title: History of the German Language
description: Development of German from its earliest stages, including historical and cultural aspects. GER 430 History of the German Language (3) This course provides an overview of the history of the German language from its origins to the present. Historical changes and dialectal variation in phonology (sound system), morphology (word structure), syntax (sentence structure), lexicon (vocabulary), and semantics (word meaning) will be examined. Particular emphasis is placed on the impact of cultural and historical changes on the development of German, including its standardization. Students will be evaluated on the basis of homework, classroom participation, tests, and an in-class presentation with a written abstract. No prior knowledge of linguistics is required. The class is conducted in German.

subject: GER
title: Dragons, the Divine and the Demonic: German Literature, Culture and Media--Medieval to 1750
description: King Arthur's knights slaying dragons, medieval mystics' visions of the divine, and the demon, Mephistopheles' tempting of Dr. Faustus are well-known themes from pre-modern cultural production in German-speaking regions. Analysis of literary and cultural production in German-speaking regions of the pre-modern period reveals how these themes function within an underlying narrative and symbolic complexity that can in turn shed light on the diverse and ever-shifting social ideals, political forces, sex and gender expression, and worldviews during this time span. Students will examine historical documents, literary works, and artistic production, as well as secondary articles, to discuss the complexity and diversity of this time period in German-speaking regions. Students will compare the medieval material with its reception in modern cultural production and will evaluate the relevance of medieval culture to modern society. The primary language for reading and discussion in this course is German.

subject: GER
title: Worlds, Wars, and the Self: German Culture from the Enlightenment to the Present
description: This course examines German literary texts and media from 1750 to the present across a wide array of genres, from short stories to dramas and even videos. Students survey seminal literary texts from the Enlightenment, like the genres of the bourgeois tragedy or the epistolary novel, before considering both canonical and lesser-known texts and visual media from the twentieth- and twenty-first centuries. While this course focuses on the German literary canon beginning in the Enlightenment, other literary works, such as those by Bertolt Brecht or Emine Sevgi Özdamar, may be discussed later in the semester in their historical context. In addition to literary texts, students may also engage with works of art, films, and other audio-visual media. The sequence of texts and media from 1750 to the present demonstrates the diverse and multicultural aspects of contemporary German culture. Ultimately, this course explores with the ways in which modern German-speaking subjects have participated in, rebelled against, or conformed to the worlds in which they live. This course is conducted primarily in German.

subject: GER
title: Varieties and dialects of German
description: This course surveys the varieties, dialects, and flavors of German around the world. The class compares and contrasts traditional dialects of German (e.g., Hochdeutsch 'Standard German') with other varieties of German (e.g., Kiezdeutsch, Namdeutsch). Students will examine the structure of these language varieties across social, stylistic, and cultural spaces. Students will gain insight into ongoing changes in the language that extend beyond what is commonly taught in textbooks. Students will also explore how German dialects differ linguistically from another and how speakers use alternate forms of German for specific purposes, meanings, and functions. This course is conducted primarily in German.

subject: GER
title: Seminar in German Culture
description: Seminar devoted to a special topic in the field of German culture and civilization.

subject: GER
title: Migration and Multilingualism
description: This course explores the politics of migration, as well as the challenges and opportunities presented by monolingualism and multilingualism in German history and culture. We will examine writing, translation, and the global traffic of texts as they form and alter linguistic and cultural landscapes. We will address questions of migration and translation in different media, such as film, literature, music, and theater. Students will also have the chance to reflect on their potential of becoming multilingual. This course will be taught primarily in German.
prereqAdvisory: GER 401Y or Ger 402 Concurrent: Prerequisite GER 401Y or Ger 402 Recommended Preparations: This course requires the ability to read, write, and speak German on the advanced level.

subject: GER
title: Horror, Terror, Fantasy
description: This course will explore major themes of horror, terror, and fantasy in German literature and culture. What are the political and psychological meanings hidden in monster stories? What is the relationship between literary and historical accounts of horror? We will examine how fantastical, spectral, supernatural, monstrous, and demonic figures haunt visual representations, literary and cinematic narratives. Our discussions will focus on the impact of historical events, such as revolutions, epidemics, war, genocide, urban life, and modern anxieties, on art and media. This course is conducted primarily in German.
extraRaw: Concurrent: GER401Y or GER 402 Recommended Preparations: The course requires an upper-level undergraduate ability to read, write, and speak German.

subject: GER
title: Sex and Media
description: This course introduces students to topics in gender and sexuality in German media, literature, film, and their cultural contexts throughout various time periods. We will explore how gender has been constructed through media in the German-speaking world and how notions of gender and sexuality put different demands on people. Topics may include portrayals of femininity, masculinity, gender fluidity, and queerness in various media (e.g., literature, music, the arts, and digital media). Students will discuss the ways in which certain behaviors or lifestyles have been stigmatized or made taboo. Students will analyze how notions of gender and sexuality interact with virtual and physical spaces, the environment, and a multicultural world. This course is conducted primarily in German. This course is repeatable up to twice because different faculty members teach the course in rotation. Faculty members will address this broad topic during different historical periods with different primary and secondary literature. In other words, students will engage with entirely different historical periods, authors and artists, media, and literature if they repeat the course.
extraRaw: Concurrent: GER 401Y or GER 402 Recommended Preparations: Intermediate to advanced knowledge of German. Recommended completion of GER 310

subject: GER
title: Forbidden Forests: Ecology and Storytelling
description: This course examines various texts and visual media from the Middle Ages to the present in which the natural world plays a central role. From haunted forests to the Green Party, and from fairy tales to modern eco-thrillers, the dangers, wonders, and fragility of the environment remain critical to the German imagination. In this course we will link media (e.g., literature, music, the arts, and digital media) to topics including environmental catastrophe, climate change, sustainability and co-existing with nature.

subject: GER
title: Romanticism
description: A study of both early and late romanticism, including such writers as Novalis, the Schlegels, E.T.A. Hoffmann, and Heine.

subject: GER
title: Introduction to German Film History and Theory in Context
description: Introduces films in German since the 1960s and addresses issues relevant to German and European cultures and politics. GER 489 Introduction to German Film History and Theory in Context (3) This course focuses on German cinema's development since the 1960s. The course situates the 'Young' and then 'New German Cinema' within contemporaneous European and U.S. film cultures. Thus the course will address the difference between the European cinematic culture of 'auteurs' versus the school of 'genres' in the U.S.The preceding traditions of Italian Neo-realism and of the Frenchnouvelle vagueare also engaged alongside a few Hungarian, Czech and/or Polish films. The students will have the opportunity to consider how these other national cinematic productions impacted the German filmmakers who were involved in the creation of a national German cinema that would critically engage Hollywood on the one hand, and distance itself from the Nazi past on the other.The course will be structured around questions about the grounds for a national cinema and its cultural and critical relevance both at the time these films were produced and today. Yet, the national question will not be the only focus of this class, in the course of which students will be able to discuss the historical, political and ethical questions raised by the directors selected. In addition, students in this course will learn about the specificity of cinematic language and will be exposed to some film theory. In conclusion, the course provides upper level undergraduate students with a basic knowledge of the most important New German films, with a confrontation with issues specifically relevant to a study of German culture, and with some familiarity with film theory.The evaluation methods for this course will be based on 1) participation [attendance; reports/worksheets, after each film and in class discussion]: 30%; 2) presentation 20%; 3) take-home mid term essay 20%; and 4) final paper 30%. The course is part of the German Program, in particular of the German Studies curriculum. It teaches students of German culture about German and European contemporary cinema, while situating the cinema within broader historical-political debates concerning Europe. It functions as an excellent complementary course to our GER LIT classes at the 400 level and offers an additional choice to pursue cultural studies to those who are more reticent about reading texts. Enrollment: 25. The course will be offered every other year.
